title: Labour representatives propose Tk 32,000 minimum wage for garment workers
summary: Labour representatives on the Minimum Wages Board have proposed a minimum monthly wage of Tk 32,000 for workers in Bangladesh's export-oriented ready-made garment (RMG) industry. The proposal was subm...
content: Labour representatives on the Minimum Wages Board have proposed a minimum monthly wage of Tk 32,000 for workers in Bangladesh's export-oriented ready-made garment (RMG) industry. The proposal was submitted at the board's second meeting on 9 November in Segunbagicha, Dhaka, amid ongoing worker protests demanding higher wages. Courtesy: Collected The workers' side proposed Tk 48,000 for Grade 1, Tk 43,000 for Grade 2, Tk 38,000 for Grade 3 and Tk 32,000 for Grade 4 workers. Newly recruited entry-level and apprentice workers would receive Tk 30,000 under the proposal. Babul Akhter, a workers' representative on the board, said the proposed wages account for inflation, rising living costs, housing rent, healthcare, and children's education. The current minimum monthly wage in the RMG sector is Tk 12,500, announced in 2023. Meanwhile, garment owners' representatives have been given four working days to submit their proposed wage structure after requesting additional time due to ongoing unrest in industrial areas. The six-member Minimum Wages Board was formed on 1 November to recommend a revised wage structure for the country's garment workers.

summary: A three-year Dutch-Bangladeshi initiative will connect regenerative cotton farming, garment waste recovery and fiber-to-fiber recycling to advance circularity across Bangladesh’s textile value chain. Bangladesh’s transition towards a circular textile industry has gained momentum with the launch of the Cotton Loop Bangladesh Impact Cluster, a three-year initiative connecting regenerative cotton cultivation with garment waste recovery and […] The post Cotton Loop Bangladesh Impact Cluster launched in Bangladesh appeared first on Textile Focus .
content: A three-year Dutch-Bangladeshi initiative will connect regenerative cotton farming, garment waste recovery and fiber-to-fiber recycling to advance circularity across Bangladesh’s textile value chain. Bangladesh’s transition towards a circular textile industry has gained momentum with the launch of the Cotton Loop Bangladesh Impact Cluster, a three-year initiative connecting regenerative cotton cultivation with garment waste recovery and fiber-to-fiber recycling. Figure 1: The Cotton Loop Bangladesh Impact Cluster, formally launched in Dhaka Formally launched in Dhaka on 4 November 2026, the initiative brings together international brands, textile manufacturers, recycling specialists, technology providers and research institutions from Bangladesh and the Netherlands. Its primary objective is to demonstrate how cotton can pass through successive production and recycling cycles while retaining its quality and commercial value, targeting two complete recycling cycles by 2029. Led by Raddis Cotton, the consortium includes Dutch partners Zeeman, Company Fits, Avans University of Applied Sciences and Common Era, alongside Bangladesh-based Reverse Resources. Advance Consulting and Clean & Unique are supporting the project as subcontractors. The initiative is funded by the Netherlands Enterprise Agency (RVO). The project addresses key challenges facing Bangladesh’s textile and apparel industry, including dependence on imported virgin cotton, inefficient textile waste recovery, and increasing international requirements for sustainability and supply chain traceability. summary: Registration has opened for the winter edition of Functional Fabric Fair powered by Performance Days, which will take place from 27-29 January 2027 at the Orange County Convention Center in Orlando, Florida. The event will run alongside the PGA Show, the golf industry’s largest annual business gathering, bringing performance textile suppliers into closer contact with […] The post Functional Fabric Fair opens Orlando registration appeared first on Knitting Industry .
content: Registration has opened for the winter edition of Functional Fabric Fair powered by Performance Days, which will take place from 27-29 January 2027 at the Orange County Convention Center in Orlando, Florida. The event will run alongside the PGA Show, the golf industry’s largest annual business gathering, bringing performance textile suppliers into closer contact with apparel brands, designers and product developers working across golf, racquet sports, outdoor and activewear markets. Expanded from two days to three, Functional Fabric Fair Winter will occupy the Tangerine Ballroom at the convention centre, adjacent to the PGA Show’s West Halls E and F. Both events will operate on the same dates and opening hours, although separate registration is required. More than 100 carefully selected exhibitors are expected to present high-performance fabrics, functional materials and textile technologies, with a particular emphasis on sustainability, durability and responsible sourcing. The exhibition will also feature its established Expert Talks programme and Trend Forum, providing insights into emerging material developments, performance requirements and sustainability trends influencing the sportswear and activewear sectors. “Golf apparel is one of the most active categories for performance fabric innovation, and brands want suppliers who deliver on function, durability and sustainability,” said Steve McCullough, Event Vice President, Functional Fabric Fair. “Placing the fair alongside the PGA Show puts those suppliers in the same building as the designers and product developers who need them, during a week when the whole golf industry is in Orlando.” The co-location reflects growing opportunities for textile manufacturers and suppliers as golf apparel increasingly draws on tech

title: All About AI: Mike Charalambous of Threedium, & Christy Raedeke of Custom Wrkshop
summary: Why fashion's "precision culture" sets an incredibly high aesthetic bar for AI tools and content to meet, and why machine readability also needs to be baked into every product. The post All About AI: Mike Charalambous of Threedium, & Christy Raedeke of Custom Wrkshop appeared first on The Interline .
content: Originally released in The Interline’s AI Report 2026 , this executive interview with Threedium and Custom Wrkshop is one of a 17-part series that sees The Interline quiz executives from companies who have either introduced new AI solutions or added meaningful new AI capabilities into their existing platforms . For more exclusive interviews, stories and opinions from different industry perspectives, and real survey feedback from voices from every level of fashion, download The AI Report 2026 . We’re observing a big disconnect (in both our own fashion-only data and in wider benchmarks from other sources) between the increasing capability and reliability of AI, in both a general sense and in discrete applications, and the lack of trust that end users place in its outputs. What does trust in your specific applications of AI look like, and how do you achieve and measure it? The fashion industry is asking AI tools “can I trust your output?” when it should be asking “what makes this tool impossible to get wrong?” Those are fundamentally different questions. The first is about confidence intervals. The second is about system design. The brands that will move fastest and with the greatest confidence aren’t the ones running the most AI pilots – they’re the ones that have been ruthless about identifying where in their value chain a wrong AI output is catastrophic, and demanding that their vendors build hard constraints around exactly those points. At Threedium, we build AI that generates physics-aware Digital Twins from images, prompts, or CAD files. Our outputs sit inside product development pipelines, packaging sign-off processes, and e-commerce content workflows at brands like L’Oréal and within LVMH group. title: Innovation must become a culture, not an occasional activity
title_ko: 혁신은 일시적인 활동이 아니라 문화가 되어야 합니다.
summary: When Bangladesh’s textile and apparel industry began its journey several decades ago, the gap in productivity and efficiency was much wider, while profit margins were relatively comfortable. At that s...
content: When Bangladesh’s textile and apparel industry began its journey several decades ago, the gap in productivity and efficiency was much wider, while profit margins were relatively comfortable. At that stage, factories could still grow without giving enough attention to continuous innovation. Figure: Engr. ATM Mahbubul Alam Milton, Executive Director, Masco Group & Member of the Steering Board, Textile Innovation Exchange (TIE). Today, the situation is very different. Margins are tighter, energy costs are increasing, competition is stronger and buyers are becoming more demanding. If we genuinely want to sustain this industry and remain competitive, there is no alternative to innovation. One of the problems is that we often make innovation sound much more difficult than it really is. We tend to confuse innovation with invention. Invention may require extensive research, technical knowledge, funding, time and patience. Innovation, however, can begin with a much simpler mindset: identifying a problem and finding a better way to solve it. Innovation does not always have to mean a breakthrough technology or a completely new product. A small process modification, better utility management, improved operating practice, smarter use of data or stronger coordination between departments can all be forms of innovation. These changes may appear small individually, but when they are practiced consistently across an organization, their combined impact can be significant. We can see this clearly in utilities, dyeing and production management. At Masco Group, for example, we have analysed our utility requirements and improvement opportunities up to 2030. title: Championing Youth & Sports: How Fakir Group is Inspiring the Next Generation
summary: When we think about the textile and apparel sector, we usually picture modern factories, export milestones, and global fashion trends. content: When we think about the textile and apparel sector, we usually picture modern factories, export milestones, and global fashion trends. But for Fakir Group, true industry leadership goes far beyond business. It is about giving back to society and building a brighter future for our youth. Recently, Fakir Group proved this dedication once again by stepping up as the Title Sponsor for the exciting Glenrich Inter-School Football Tournament 2026, hosted by Glenrich International School, Satarkul. A Grand Kick-Off in Dhaka The opening ceremony at the Glenrich International School auditorium was an absolute celebration of energy, color, and youthful spirit. Bringing together 18 top schools from across Dhaka, the event felt like a true festival of sports and unity. From lively school band performances to colorful flag displays and dance acts, the atmosphere was electric. For readers of Textile Focus, it is wonderful to see how corporate leaders like Fakir Group are creating positive, healthy platforms where young students can shine outside the classroom. Inspiring Words from Leadership A major highlight of the opening day was the inspiring speech by Mr. Suman Kanti Singha, Chief Human Resources Officer (CHRO) of Fakir Group. Speaking directly to the eager young athletes, teachers, and parents, he shared a powerful message about teamwork and character: “Remember that football is much more than just winning or losing a match. It is a school of life. Play hard, but play fair. Play tough, but never play rough.” His words struck a chord with everyone, encouraging the players to value sportsmanship and respect above all else. title: Overcoming the polypropylene dyeing barrier
title_ko: 폴리프로필렌 염색 장벽 극복
summary: Japan’s Prime Polymer and US biomaterials specialist Newlight Technologies have developed a new textile material that combines the lightweight properties of polypropylene (PP) with dyeability comparable to polyester. The development could significantly expand the use of PP in apparel and footwear, where its low density, durability and moisture management properties have long been attractive, but […] The post Overcoming the polypropylene dyeing barrier appeared first on Innovation in Textiles .
content: Japan’s Prime Polymer and US biomaterials specialist Newlight Technologies have developed a new textile material that combines the lightweight properties of polypropylene (PP) with dyeability comparable to polyester. The development could significantly expand the use of PP in apparel and footwear, where its low density, durability and moisture management properties have long been attractive, but its resistance to conventional dyeing processes has restricted its adoption. PP is one of the lightest commercially available textile polymers, with a density of approximately 0.91 g/cm³ compared to around 1.38 g/cm³ for polyester. It also absorbs very little moisture, making it particularly suitable for next-to-skin garments, sportswear and applications where rapid drying is important. Its highly crystalline, non-polar molecular structure, however, makes it extremely difficult to dye using conventional textile processes. As a result, PP fibres are generally coloured by adding pigments to the polymer melt before extrusion, limiting flexibility in colour selection and subsequent fabric processing. The newly developed material combines Prime Polymer’s PP alloy design and compounding expertise with Newlight’s Aircarbon polyhydroxybutyrate (PHB), a biologically produced polymer manufactured using microorganisms that convert methane into useful materials. The resulting polymer alloy can be processed from compound pellets into yarns and subsequently converted into knitted or woven fabrics. Crucially, the companies report that the resulting textiles can be dyed using conventional disperse dye systems, achieving colouration comparable to that of polyester. title: Before Bangladesh sells its future, it must build the ecosystem behind it
summary: Two expos in November will bring together the factories, technology providers, engineers and buyers the industry’s next phase depends on. Their legacy will be measured in what those connections produc...
content: Two expos in November will bring together the factories, technology providers, engineers and buyers the industry’s next phase depends on. Their legacy will be measured in what those connections produce. Figure 1: TIE-ITET Textile Innovation Expo 2026 Press meet was held on 12 October 2026. Between January and July 2026, the average import value per kilogram of Bangladeshi apparel entering the European Union fell by 8.47 per cent from a year earlier, while Vietnam’s rose by 11.76 per cent, according to Eurostat figures cited at a Dhaka press briefing in October. Product mix can exaggerate such gaps, but the direction is hard to ignore. It sharpens the question this November puts to the industry: how can Bangladesh’s factories create more value, and keep more of it? November offers a chance to work on the answer. Days apart, Dhaka will host two gatherings that address different parts of the industry’s next phase. The TIE-ITET Textile Innovation Expo 2026 runs from 12 to 14 November at International Convention City Bashundhara. BATEXPO, which BGMEA is reviving for its silver jubilee edition after a gap since 2013, follows on 18 and 19 November at the Bangladesh-China Friendship Conference Center. Until recently, 24 November was also the date set for Bangladesh to leave the least developed country category. On 29 October, the UN General Assembly extended the preparatory period by three years, moving graduation to 24 November 2029. The extension buys time. It does not change what factories can make or earn. Ready-made garment exports earned $38.70 billion in 2025-26, 1.64 per cent less than the year before. title: Lululemon unveils thermoregulating running vest
summary: Lululemon has introduced its Ventscape PrimaLoft ThermoPlume+ Run Vest, a new performance apparel innovation designed to help runners maintain thermal comfort in changing conditions without the need to adjust or remove layers. Unveiled at the 2026 China International Import Expo, the vest features a patent-pending construction that combines lightweight insulation with strategically positioned mesh panels […] The post Lululemon unveils thermoregulating running vest appeared first on Knitting Industry .
content: Lululemon has introduced its Ventscape PrimaLoft ThermoPlume+ Run Vest, a new performance apparel innovation designed to help runners maintain thermal comfort in changing conditions without the need to adjust or remove layers. Unveiled at the 2026 China International Import Expo, the vest features a patent-pending construction that combines lightweight insulation with strategically positioned mesh panels to regulate warmth, airflow and moisture during cold-weather running. Developed in collaboration with Lululemon’s athlete ambassadors, the Ventscape Run Vest is designed to address a common challenge for runners: maintaining a comfortable body temperature as physical exertion and environmental conditions change. The construction uses PrimaLoft ThermoPlume+ insulation to provide warmth at the beginning of a run, when the body is generating less heat. As running intensity increases, strategically placed mesh vents allow air to circulate through the garment, releasing accumulated heat and humidity from the microclimate surrounding the body. According to Lululemon, the combination of insulation and ventilation creates a more consistent thermal experience, reducing the need for runners to stop and adjust their clothing. “Our Ambassadors expressed a common theme of how running in cold weather creates peaks and dips related to thermal discomfort,” said Chantelle Murnaghan, Vice President of Research and Product Innovation at Lululemon. “We wanted to create a solution that allows runners to embrace the weather and not view it in a negative way. title_ko: Unspun과 Arvind Limited 간의 랜드마크 파트너십
summary: AHMEDABAD, India & SAN FRANCISCO — November 9, 2026 — unspun, the B Corp-certified fashion technology company behind OneWeave™ 3D weaving, and Arvind Limited, one of India’s leading textile-to-retail conglomerates, today announced a strategic partnership to bring yarn-to-garment 3D weaving into industrial-scale apparel manufacturing. The deployment marks Arvind’s first installation of OneWeave™ technology and the […]
content: AHMEDABAD, India & SAN FRANCISCO — November 9, 2026 — unspun, the B Corp-certified fashion technology company behind OneWeave 3D weaving, and Arvind Limited, one of India’s leading textile-to-retail conglomerates, today announced a strategic partnership to bring yarn-to-garment 3D weaving into industrial-scale apparel manufacturing. The deployment marks Arvind’s first installation of OneWeave technology and the first time unspun’s 3D weaving platform will move from its own microfactory into the production environment of a global Tier-1 manufacturer — an important step in the company’s broader vision for more responsive, automated and lower-waste apparel supply chains. The fashion industry’s operating model still depends heavily on forecasting demand months in advance, committing to bulk orders, and correcting for inevitable misses through markdowns, deadstock and disposal. McKinsey has reported that U.S. retailers alone were sitting on approximately $740 billion in unsold goods in 2023. As of July 19, 2026, new EU rules prohibit large companies from destroying unsold clothes, clothing accessories and footwear across the EU — a policy shift that makes overproduction not just a sustainability problem, but a compliance and business-model risk. In apparel manufacturing, conventional cut-and-sew production also creates fabric offcuts before a garment ever reaches a customer — making waste, excess inventory and long lead times structural problems rather than edge cases. Under the partnership, Arvind will deploy two OneWeave machines at its facility in Ahmedabad, India, with operations expected to begin by December 2026. The cloud-based platform has been introduced as part of Missoni’s decision to bring the management of its Missoni Home business in-house, requiring […] The post Lectra PLM cuts time for Missoni appeared first on Innovation in Textiles .
content: Italian fashion and home textiles brand Missoni has reduced the time spent managing and maintaining product data by an estimated 60% following the implementation of Lectra’s Kubix Link product lifecycle management (PLM) system. The cloud-based platform has been introduced as part of Missoni’s decision to bring the management of its Missoni Home business in-house, requiring new operational processes and closer integration between product development, production, quality control and supply chain partners. Founded in 1953 by Ottavio and Rosita Missoni, the Milan-based company is internationally recognised for its distinctive knitwear, colours and geometric patterns. Its activities have expanded beyond fashion into home textiles, furnishings and accessories. Missoni has worked with Lectra for more than 25 years, initially introducing the company’s CAD solutions in the early 2000s. The latest project involved implementing Kubix Link to centralise product information and establish a common platform for managing collections and coordinating activities across departments. Following an initial analysis phase, the system went live after a 12-month implementation period and has since been adopted by more than 40 users across product development, merchandising, quality control and compliance. More than 20 suppliers and subcontractors have also been given direct access to technical product information, reducing the need for email exchanges and improving coordination throughout the supply chain. Missoni now manages more than 20,000 stock keeping units (SKUs) through the system and creates almost 1,000 new items annually. content: LEONBERG, Germany — November 9, 2026 — With rising energy costs, increasing environmental requirements, and growing competitive pressure, textile manufacturers worldwide are facing the challenge of making their production processes both more sustainable and more cost-effective. As one of the world’s leading specialists in textile finishing machinery, Brückner will present innovative solutions and advanced production technologies at ITMA ASIA 2026 in Shanghai. These technologies can play a key role in significantly reducing both energy consumption and emissions. A special focus will be placed on the company’s proven heat recovery and exhaust air purification systems. These solutions enable manufacturers to recover valuable energy from production processes, substantially reduce overall energy demand, and reliably comply with environmental regulations at the same time. For many textile finishers, they offer considerable potential for lowering operating costs and reducing CO₂ emissions. POWER-FRAME stenter equipped with heat recovery and exhaust air purification system Brückner will also demonstrate how modern stenter technology can make a significant contribution to resource-efficient production. The latest generation of the POWER-FRAME stenter combines outstanding process quality with numerous features designed to maximize energy efficiency. Optimized airflow systems, highly efficient burner technology, intelligent control and automation solutions, and innovative energy-saving packages help significantly reduce energy consumption and operating costs while increasing productivity. “Sustainability has long become a decisive competitive factor for many textile companies. content: The British Textile Machinery Association (BTMA) is looking to India ITME 2026 as a major opportunity to strengthen industrial partnerships and mutually expand exports, following the introduction of the UK-India Free Trade Agreement and the formation of the UK-India Textile Machinery Coalition (UKITMC). Taking place from December 4-9th at the India Exposition Mart in Greater Noida, the exhibition is expected to attract more than 1,800 exhibitors and 150,000 visitors, reflecting India’s position as one of the worl’’s largest textile manufacturing markets. The event comes at a significant moment for trade relations between the two countries. The Free Trade Agreement, which entered into force in July 2026, is expected to improve market access and competitiveness for British engineering and technology suppliers, while supporting the continued expansion of India’s textile and apparel industries. The BTMA has also established the UKITMC to strengthen cooperation between machinery manufacturers in the two countries, encourage technology exchange and develop new commercial opportunities. “India represents an enormous opportunity for British textile machinery manufacturers, particularly as its textile industry moves towards higher levels of automation, quality assurance and sustainable production,” says BTMA CEO Jason Kent. “The combination of the Free Trade Agreement and our new coalition provides a much stronger framework for long-term collaboration. content: Groz-Beckert, the German manufacturer of industrial needles, precision components and textile machinery accessories, will introduce new developments across all of its six principal product areas, at ITMA Asia + CITME 2026, taking place in Shanghai from November 20-24th. A specific emphasis will be on reducing energy consumption, extending component service life and improving processing performance. Among the highlights is a new energy-saving, maintenance-free cylinder wire for spinning applications, designed to increase card output while reducing maintenance requirements and extending operating life. Further developments in stationary flats and revolving tops can improve carding performance, including new configurations for processing fine yarns and adapting to the latest generation of carding machines. In circular knitting, Groz-Beckert will highlight its LCmax needle technology, which employs a wave-shaped shank geometry to reduce friction and energy consumption during operation. The company is also addressing the growing complexity of technical and medical textiles with its San TT flat knitting needle, developed specifically for producing particularly tight stitch structures. Another development, the San FY, is designed to improve processing reliability and fabric appearance when working with irregular effect yarns. Fine-gauge knitting technology will be demonstrated in collaboration with Chinese flat knitting machine specialist Sinotex, with a knitted collar illustrating the potential for producing finer fabrics and tighter stitch structures. Glass yarn demands Technical textiles are also a focus of the company’s weaving developments, particularly in the production of fabrics used in printed circuit boards and other electronic applications. title: NBR proposes income tax reduction to 15% for textile sector until 2030
summary: The National Board of Revenue (NBR) has proposed reducing the income tax rate for Bangladesh’s textile sector from 27.5% to 15%, aiming to ease financial pressure on domestic mills and enhance their c...
content: The National Board of Revenue (NBR) has proposed reducing the income tax rate for Bangladesh’s textile sector from 27.5% to 15%, aiming to ease financial pressure on domestic mills and enhance their competitiveness. If approved, the reduced tax rate will remain effective until 30 June 2030, providing long-term support to the country’s textile industry. The tax authority has prepared a draft statutory regulatory order (SRO) and sent it to Finance Minister Amir Khosru Mahmud Chowdhury for approval. A senior finance official said the SRO would be issued shortly after receiving approval. In its proposal, sent to the finance minister on 5 November, the NBR recommended the reduced rate under Section 76(1) of the Income Tax Act, citing the need to protect exports and employment and ensure sustainable growth of the textile industry. According to the NBR, the textile sector covers yarn production, yarn dyeing, finishing, coning, fabric dyeing, printing and other related activities. The sector previously enjoyed a 15% income tax rate under an SRO introduced in 2015 for a 10-year period. However, after the order expired in 2025, the tax rate reverted to 27.5%. In May this year, the Bangladesh Textile Mills Association (BTMA) proposed reducing the income tax rate to 10% until 2030. The association argued that the export-oriented ready-made garment (RMG) sector continues to enjoy a 12% tax rate, creating a disparity between the two interconnected industries. However, the NBR did not consider the proposal while preparing the current fiscal year's budget. The latest tax reduction proposal comes amid mounting operational and financial challenges facing domestic textile mills. title: Fiber traceability turns transparency into business value for spinning mills
title_ko: 섬유 추적성은 투명성을 방적 공장의 비즈니스 가치로 전환합니다.
summary: For spinning mills, fiber traceability is moving beyond a buyer compliance exercise. It is becoming a business strategy. Brands need stronger evidence behind sustainability claims, while regulations a...
content: For spinning mills, fiber traceability is moving beyond a buyer compliance exercise. It is becoming a business strategy. Brands need stronger evidence behind sustainability claims, while regulations are pushing supply chains toward structured product information. This places spinning mills between raw fiber suppliers and garment manufacturers. Figure: Textile Exchange's Materials Market Report 2026 estimates that global fiber production reached 139 million tons in 2025, up from 132 million tons in 2024. Courtesy: Collected The fiber market is growing, but proof is lagging Textile Exchange's Materials Market Report 2026 estimates that global fiber production reached 139 million tons in 2025, up from 132 million tons in 2024. Polyester remained dominant at 82.5 million tons, or 59% of total production. Recycled polyester reached 9.7 million tons, but 97% came from plastic bottles. Textile-to-textile recycled fibers accounted for only 0.76% of global fiber production. Cotton production reached 25.7 million tons; 9.4 million tons, or 37% of virgin cotton, came through certified programs. These figures highlight the challenge. Brands want more recycled and preferred materials, but suppliers must prove fiber origin, composition, and movement. Mills that provide reliable batch-level evidence can differentiate their yarn, support higher-value orders, and reduce repeated buyer verification. Digital records need physical evidence A digital traceability system links each fiber or yarn batch with its supplier, origin, certification, lot number, blend ratio, input weight, production stage, and output volume. summary: Texworld Apparel Sourcing Paris will celebrate its 30th anniversary from 25-27 January 2027 at the Paris-Le-Bourget Exhibition Centre, bringing together international fabric manufacturers, garment producers and sourcing professionals. Organised by Messe Frankfurt France, the anniversary edition will introduce a redesigned layout across Halls 3 and 4, aimed at strengthening connections between fabrics and finished products […] The post Texworld Paris marks 30th anniversary appeared first on Knitting Industry .
content: Texworld Apparel Sourcing Paris will celebrate its 30th anniversary from 25-27 January 2027 at the Paris-Le-Bourget Exhibition Centre, bringing together international fabric manufacturers, garment producers and sourcing professionals. Organised by Messe Frankfurt France, the anniversary edition will introduce a redesigned layout across Halls 3 and 4, aimed at strengthening connections between fabrics and finished products while improving visitor navigation. The new configuration will accommodate the event’s two principal areas: Texworld, dedicated to fabrics and raw materials, and Apparel Sourcing, which focuses on finished garments and accessories. Networking spaces, trend forums, conference areas and visitor services will be distributed across both halls to encourage interaction between exhibitors and buyers. More than 1,000 international exhibitors are expected, offering a broad selection of textile materials and finished products. Strong participation is anticipated from Indian manufacturers, reflecting growing interest in the European market and the potential opportunities arising from the proposed EU-India free trade agreement. The agreement, currently undergoing ratification and expected to enter into force in 2027, could eliminate European import duties on Indian textiles and garments, which currently reach up to 12% depending on the product. Trend forums dedicated to Spring/Summer 2028 collections will feature in both exhibition halls. Developed by artistic directors Louis Gérin and Gregory Lamaud, they will present creative directions aligned with the products on display, helping buyers identify emerging trends and sourcing opportunities. title: INDA Announces New Name For International Fiber Journal
title_ko: INDA, International Fiber Journal의 새로운 이름 발표
summary: CARY, N.C. — November 9, 2026 — INDA, the Association of the Nonwoven Fabrics Industry, and its publishing arm INDA Media are excited to announce that International Fiber Journal (IFJ) will become Fibers&Nonwovens with Issue 1, 2027. The new name reflects the magazine’s longstanding focus on fiber innovation and its coverage of the materials, technologies […]
content: CARY, N.C. — November 9, 2026 — INDA, the Association of the Nonwoven Fabrics Industry, and its publishing arm INDA Media are excited to announce that International Fiber Journal (IFJ) will become Fibers&Nonwovens with Issue 1, 2027. The new name reflects the magazine’s longstanding focus on fiber innovation and its coverage of the materials, technologies and markets shaping the global nonwovens industry. Under its new name, the magazine will continue to deliver the industry reporting, market insights and technical perspectives that IFJ readers rely on. “Fibers, materials science, nonwovens and engineered materials have long been part of the same story for our readers,” said Rachael Davis, publisher and chief content officer, INDA Media. “An advance in fiber technology can change how a nonwoven is made, how it performs and where it can be used. Our job is to follow those connections and help readers understand what new developments mean for their work. The name Fibers&Nonwovens makes that editorial focus clear while carrying forward the technical reporting and industry perspectives readers have come to expect from International Fiber Journal.” INDA acquired International Fiber Journal and International Filtration News in October 2018. At the time, IFJ covered man-made fibers, technical textiles and nonwovens, connecting producers of engineered materials and machinery with fiber and yarn users in more than 90 countries. Current subscribers will continue to receive the new magazine without interruption. For subscription information, please email circulation@inda.org. The 2027 Media Kit is now available. summary: ALPHARETTA, Ga. — November 9, 2026 — Arclin, a materials science company, today announced the expansion of its exclusive partnership with KINETIXX, asupplier of advanced composite engineering and manufacturing, extending the reach of Kevlar® EXO™ unidirectional (UD) technology into additional high-performance consumer markets worldwide. content: ALPHARETTA, Ga. — November 9, 2026 — Arclin, a materials science company, today announced the expansion of its exclusive partnership with KINETIXX, asupplier of advanced composite engineering and manufacturing, extending the reach of Kevlar® EXO unidirectional (UD) technology into additional high-performance consumer markets worldwide. Building on a partnership first established in January 2025, the new agreement sets the stage for a new wave of product innovation beyond sporting goods. By combining Arclin’s Kevlar® EXO aramid fiber with KINETIXX’s proprietary resin matrix engineering, advanced UD prepreg development, and utility-patented hybrid composite manufacturing technologies, the companies are creating new opportunities to commercialize lightweight, high-strength composite structures across multiple industries. The agreement broadens KINETIXX’s worldwide UD exclusivity rights to cover hard luggage, bicycle structural components, and footwear applications, including fashion, sport, and work boots. The expanded agreement reinforces KINETIXX’s position as an exclusive technology partner for Kevlar® EXO UD composite applications in these categories, combining advanced material science with proprietary engineering and manufacturing capabilities developed through decades of high-performance composite innovation. title: PKSF disburses Tk2,500 crore to support 50,000 cottage and micro entrepreneurs
summary: Palli Karma-Sahayak Foundation (PKSF) has disbursed Tk2,500 crore to support around 50,000 cottage and micro entrepreneurs. Women account for 87% of the beneficiaries. Figure: PKSF disburses Tk2,500...
content: Palli Karma-Sahayak Foundation (PKSF) has disbursed Tk2,500 crore to support around 50,000 cottage and micro entrepreneurs. Women account for 87% of the beneficiaries. Figure: PKSF disburses Tk2,500 crore to support 50,000 cottage and micro entrepreneurs. Courtesy: Collected The loans were distributed through 101 partner organizations under the Special Fund for Creating Entrepreneurs in the Cottage and Micro Sectors (SOPAN) program. Bangladesh Bank is providing a Tk5,000 crore incentive package for the program, according to a PKSF press release issued on 8 November. The program covers all 64 districts and supports four sectors: technology-driven agriculture and agro-processing, manufacturing, services, and value chain financing. It aims to create new entrepreneurs and help existing microenterprises expand their businesses. It also supports production, processing, and marketing activities. PKSF received its first Tk1,250 crore tranche from Bangladesh Bank on 7 September. So far, the foundation has received Tk3,750 crore in three tranches. It expects to receive the remaining amount by December 2026. The full Tk5,000 crore fund is expected to reach entrepreneurs by January 2027. The program aims to provide more financial support to women and young entrepreneurs. It also aims to strengthen rural businesses and create jobs in rural and marginalised communities.

title: Bangladesh must move from manufacturing strength to value creation and innovation
summary: Bangladesh has built a strong position in the global apparel sourcing landscape through manufacturing scale, cost competitiveness, workforce experience and a deep supplier ecosystem. But as global sou...
content: Bangladesh has built a strong position in the global apparel sourcing landscape through manufacturing scale, cost competitiveness, workforce experience and a deep supplier ecosystem. But as global sourcing priorities evolve, the country’s future competitiveness will depend increasingly on speed, flexibility, product development, innovation, sustainability and the ability to create more value within the supply chain. content: The global denim industry is facing growing pressure to reduce its use of potassium permanganate (PP), a chemical widely used to create faded and vintage effects in denim garments. In response, CHT Group is providing technical support to the PP-free Denim Mission, an industry initiative developed by Ruess Group to accelerate the adoption of scalable alternatives to conventional PP-based finishing processes. Caption The mission aims to promote production methods that can deliver consistent denim fading effects without relying on potassium permanganate. With CHT Group's technical expertise, the initiative seeks to support the industry's transition towards safer chemical management and commercially viable finishing technologies. The scale of the challenge is significant. An industry report estimates that nearly 2,000 tons of potassium permanganate are used in denim finishing each year globally. Separately, CHT estimates that global production consumes around 250,000 liters of permanganate solution daily. PP use raises concerns over worker exposure, chemical handling, and wastewater management. Its inclusion in the Zero Discharge of Hazardous Chemicals (ZDHC) Chemical Watchlist in 2026 is also increasing industry attention on alternatives. Several technologies are being explored, including enzyme-based bleaching, laser and ozone finishing. However, replacing PP requires more than introducing another chemical. Alternative processes must deliver consistent fading effects, maintain garment quality, and remain commercially viable at industrial scale. A separate denim finishing study by Environmental Impact Measuring (EIM) and BCome demonstrated the potential of alternative technologies. title: US Cotton export sales rise on strong demand from Vietnam, Pakistan and Turkiye
summary: US cotton export sales strengthened during the week ended October 29, driven by robust demand from Vietnam, Pakistan and Turkiye. Net sales of Upland cotton for the 2026-27 marketing year increased 28...
content: US cotton export sales strengthened during the week ended October 29, driven by robust demand from Vietnam, Pakistan and Turkiye. Net sales of Upland cotton for the 2026-27 marketing year increased 28% to 277,500 running bales (RB), up from 216,500 RB in the previous week and 53% above the previous four-week average. Courtesy: Collected Vietnam emerged as the largest buyer, purchasing 200,500 RB, followed by Pakistan with 30,700 RB and Turkiye with 18,300 RB. Peru and India also recorded notable purchases. Vietnam's buying surged significantly from 35,000 RB in the previous week, while China did not feature among the major buyers. Despite stronger sales, Upland cotton export shipments fell 14% to a marketing-year low of 137,800 RB, down from 160,800 RB a week earlier and 16% below the previous four-week average. Vietnam remained the leading shipment destination with 43,500 RB, followed by Mexico, Pakistan, Bangladesh and India. Meanwhile, demand for US Pima cotton rebounded sharply. Net sales rose to 6,400 RB from just 100 RB in the previous week, with India leading purchases at 2,500 RB, followed by Bangladesh with 2,300 RB. Peru, Japan and Indonesia also contributed to the increase. Pima cotton export shipments more than doubled to 7,100 RB from 3,300 RB in the previous week. Bangladesh was the largest destination, receiving 2,200 RB, ahead of India, Vietnam, China and Thailand. The latest figures indicate continued momentum in US cotton sales, supported by strong demand from major Asian markets. However, the decline in Upland shipments highlights ongoing challenges in export execution despite improving buying interest.

title: One in three pairs, and the test that comes next
summary: One in every three pairs of denim trousers worn in the EU is made in Bangladesh. The line has been repeated so often that it risks losing its meaning. The latest Eurostat figures deserve a slower read...
content: One in every three pairs of denim trousers worn in the EU is made in Bangladesh. The line has been repeated so often that it risks losing its meaning. The latest Eurostat figures deserve a slower reading. Between January and August, Bangladesh shipped €869.13 million of denim to the bloc, a 29.40 percent share, and stayed first, about €344 million ahead of Pakistan. Shipments still fell 5.85 percent, slightly faster than the market's 4.40 percent decline, and the share slipped from 29.85 percent. August offered relief, with a 12.71 percent rise year on year. Rivals fared worse: Turkey lost 21.08 percent, Morocco 14.48, Pakistan 7.88. Yet Egypt grew 31.46 percent and Vietnam 45.38, both from small bases. So, the rank is safe for now, but the cushion is not guaranteed. One good month does not make a trend, and a leader that shrinks a little in a shrinking market should not mistake its position for a plan. What turns a position into a plan? A small clue came from Envoy Textiles' mill in Bhaluka on 17 October, when the sustainability teams of American Eagle Outfitters and Li & Fung, led by Michelle Tarry, spent the day there. Discussions covered the mill's hydropower project, stenter heat recovery and biogas plant, along with decarbonization, water stewardship, traceability and sustainable materials. No order was announced, and none should be assumed. That is what makes the visit worth noting. A brand and its sourcing partner sent sustainability specialists, not buyers, to a denim mill. Price gets a mill onto the shortlist. Evidence of what went into every meter of fabric keeps it there. Bangladeshi industry voices point the same way. Photo credit: Military Women’s Memorial For more than 60 years, Milliken & Company fabric has been part of U.S. military uniforms worn by generations of service members, including many of the women honored at the Military Women’s Memorial. As founding sponsor of the Memorial’s new uniform exhibit, the Milliken & Company Charitable Foundation will help share the stories of women who have served in the U.S. Armed Forces, using the same craftsmanship and connection to service that has defined our military partnership since World War II. content: EVANSTON, Ill. — November 4, 2026 — NylaNova, a chemical recycling company built on technology from Northwestern University, today announced a partnership with Nylene under which NylaNova will supply Nylene with green caprolactam recovered from post-consumer nylon-6 waste. Caprolactam is the raw material used to make nylon, and Nylene is an established nylon-6 producer with operations in the United States and Canada. Nylene has been producing specialty nylon resins, copolymers, and compounds for decades, supplying the automotive, packaging, wire and cable, injection molding, roto molding, fiber, and carpet industries. The company is also long established in nylon recycling, operating a nylon-6 depolymerization process at its Arnprior, Ontario facility, one of only three such units in the world and the longest continuously running. Under the partnership, NylaNova’s green caprolactam becomes an additional supply source for their nylon-6 production. It is an important step as NylaNova builds a broader network of partners to bring recycled nylon-6 back into production. Yosi Kratish, Founder and CTO of NylaNova Nylon-6 is used across apparel, carpet, and industrial applications, and roughly 2.75 million tonnes of it are discarded worldwide each year. Almost none of that material is turned back into nylon, making it one of the most difficult plastics to return to the supply chain. At the same time, recycled-content requirements are tightening. Mandates are now law in California and New York, textile and carpet EPR bills are advancing in six more states, and EU textile EPR schemes must be in place by April 2028. content: A pair of stretch jeans offers comfort, flexibility, and a better fit. A small amount of elastane helps denim stretch and recover its shape after wear. However, this performance comes with an end-of-life challenge. When blended with cotton, elastane can complicate textile recycling and limit the recovery of usable fibers. The challenge for denim manufacturers is to preserve comfort while designing garments for a more circular future. Figure: Italian denim manufacturer Candiani Denim developed COREVA technology using natural rubber yarn instead of synthetic stretch yarn. Courtesy: Collected Elastane, also known as spandex, is difficult to separate from other fibers using many existing recycling technologies. Mechanical recycling shreds fabric into fibers, which can become shorter and weaker. Even low elastane content can disrupt textile-to-textile recycling, according to Fashion for Good. Its Stretching Circularity project, launched in February 2026, is evaluating bio-based and recycled elastane alternatives alongside technologies for separating and recovering blended fibers. The project aims to generate comparable data on performance, environmental impact, commercial feasibility, and scalability. Reconsidering fabric construction The first step is to reconsider where stretch is necessary. Mechanical stretch uses yarn structure, twist, and fabric construction to provide flexibility without a separate elastic fiber. Low-elastane designs offer another option for products that need limited stretch and recovery. However, manufacturers must test durability, fit retention, fabric growth, and recovery after repeated wear and washing before adopting these approaches commercially. title: EU makes product identifiers mandatory for e-commerce imports from November
summary: The European Union (EU) has made product identifiers mandatory for goods sold through online distance sales and declared for customs from November 1, 2026. The new requirement covers all 27 EU member...
content: The European Union (EU) has made product identifiers mandatory for goods sold through online distance sales and declared for customs from November 1, 2026. The new requirement covers all 27 EU member states and aims to improve product traceability, strengthen customs enforcement, and detect unsafe or non-compliant imports. Figure: The requirement follows EU-wide customs control actions that identified numerous low-value goods purchased online from outside the bloc that failed to meet EU product safety and compliance requirements. Under the new rules, customs declarations must include three product identifiers: a merchant product identifier (M-PID), a non-standardized manufacturer product identifier (NS-PID), and a standardized manufacturer product identifier (S-PID). The European Commission introduced the requirements to help customs authorities identify specific products more accurately and improve controls on goods entering the EU through e-commerce channels. The M-PID identifies a product's listing on a specific website, marketplace, or online platform. It is assigned by the seller or platform and helps customs trace the exact product offer. The NS-PID connects a product to its manufacturer and model through references such as style, model, or part numbers. The S-PID provides an internationally recognized product reference, usually through a barcode such as an EAN or UPC. These identifiers will allow customs authorities to track the same product across different online platforms, even when it is sold by different merchants. If a product is found to be unsafe or non-compliant, authorities can extend their controls to other products presenting similar risks. title: Cascale reports 22% emission cuts among factories engaged with Higg FEM
summary: Cascale has reported a 22% reduction in emissions over four years among factories that maintained engagement with its Higg Facility Environmental Module (FEM). The industry alliance announced the find...
content: Cascale has reported a 22% reduction in emissions over four years among factories that maintained engagement with its Higg Facility Environmental Module (FEM). The industry alliance announced the findings on November 5, alongside the launch of the 2026 update of Higg FEM. The updated assessment aims to strengthen environmental performance measurement and support manufacturers in tracking improvements. It introduces a standalone environmental baseline assessment, stronger water-data checks, and integrated guidance for manufacturers. The standalone baseline assessment is a key change in the updated framework. It provides a starting point for facilities to assess their environmental performance before tracking progress over time. Cascale has also strengthened its water-data checks to improve the quality and reliability of reported information. Better data can help manufacturers identify environmental gaps and make more informed decisions about resource management. The updated module also includes integrated guidance to help manufacturers understand the assessment requirements and improve their environmental performance. The reported 22% emissions reduction highlights the importance of continued factory participation in environmental assessment programs. It also indicates that regular engagement and performance tracking can support measurable progress in reducing industrial emissions. For the textile and apparel industry, the update puts greater emphasis on data quality, environmental baselines and continuous improvement at the factory level.

content: TÜBINGEN, Germany — November 4, 2026 — CHT Germany GmbH, part of the foundation-owned CHT Group, is a finalist for the “German Sustainability Award Companies 2027” in the Large Companies size class. The CHT Group is proud that the jury has selected the company for this prestigious award. The finalist recognition honors the CHT Group’s extensive efforts to advance sustainable transformation across product development and industrial applications. The jury was particularly impressed by the integration of chemical product development with industrial customer processes. It highlights the PIGMENTURA textile dyeing process using a pad-dry process as an approach to reducing water consumption. The jury also recognizes the CHT Group’s work on product carbon footprints and its systematic assessment of critical substances. Within the CHT Group, a calculation tool supports the assessment of product carbon footprints as early as the product development stage. In addition, a science-based internal classification system helps identify critical substances and replace them wherever technically and economically feasible. In this way, the CHT Group incorporates key sustainability considerations from the development stage onward, connecting process design, transparency, and substance selection with the requirements of industrial applications. Being a finalist for the German Sustainability Award Companies affirms the CHT Group’s approach and recognizes the efforts made to date toward a more sustainable chemical industry. title: Data, circularity and value shape Bangladesh’s next chapter in Europe
summary: For years, Europe has been one of Bangladesh’s most dependable growth engines. But the European market that helped build Bangladesh’s apparel export success is changing rapidly and the warning signs a...
content: For years, Europe has been one of Bangladesh’s most dependable growth engines. But the European market that helped build Bangladesh’s apparel export success is changing rapidly and the warning signs are already visible in the numbers. In the first half of 2026, Bangladesh’s apparel exports to the European Union fell 16.43% year-on-year to €8.64 billion, according to Eurostat data. Export volume declined 8.22%, while average export prices fell 8.94%. The EU itself was a weaker market: total apparel imports from global suppliers fell 9.7% to €41.1 billion. But Bangladesh’s decline was considerably sharper than the market contraction. That makes the current European slowdown more than a cyclical demand problem. It raises a bigger question: Is Bangladesh losing competitiveness in its most important export market just as Europe redefines what “competitive” means? The answer will depend on whether Bangladesh treats Europe’s new regulatory environment simply as another compliance burden or as a catalyst for a different manufacturing model. From volume to value Europe’s buyers are under pressure. Bangladesh is under greater pressure. European apparel demand has weakened, prices have softened and competition among sourcing countries has intensified. Yet the most revealing comparison from H1 2026 is not Bangladesh’s 16.43% decline alone. It is what happened to competitors. Vietnam’s apparel exports to the EU increased 0.36% in value even though its shipment volume fell 11.52%. Its average export price, meanwhile, increased 13.43%. Bangladesh, by contrast, experienced declines in both volume and average price. That contrast points towards the central challenge facing Bangladesh. content: MÖNCHENGLADBACH, Germany— November 5, 2026 — Faster support, shorter downtime and advanced repair capabilities: customers across Pakistan can now benefit from the Trützschler Service Station at its new location in Lahore. By combining Trützschler service expertise with state-of-the-art diagnostic equipment, the new facility helps spinning mills resolve technical issues more quickly and maintain reliable production. Left to right: Markus Wurster (Director Markets), Nadeem Tahir (Trützschler Service Technician), Simon Rameiser (Head of Customer Service), Mohammad Riaz (Trützschler Service Technician) and Nico Sieben (Area Manager Pakistan) inside the Trützschler Service Station in Lahore. Located directly in the center of Gulberg, Lahore, the new location brings the Trützschler Service Station and the sales agency Machpart together under one roof. Now, the Service Station offers expanded technical capabilities, including troubleshooting, repair services, technical inspections and customer support for Trützschler spinning preparation equipment. An emergency spare parts stock further helps reduce downtime by enabling the rapid replacement of components. Professional repair standards close to the customer Equipped with advanced testing and diagnostic equipment, the new facility allows the team to inspect, analyze, and repair electronic components to the same high standards applied throughout the global Trützschler service network. A particular benefit for customers is Trützschler’s proactive repair approach. Rather than simply replacing a failed component, service technicians inspect related parts and assemblies for potential damage or wear. Sampaio, RDD Textiles, Tintex Textiles, FOV Fabrics, Utenos Trikotažas and Swisstex Direct […] The post Reju strengthens regenerated polyester supply chain appeared first on Knitting Industry .
content: Reju is working with six textile mills in Europe and the Americas to develop finished fabrics from regenerated polyester, as it prepares to establish an international network of industrial-scale textile recycling facilities. The Paris-based company, owned by Technip Energies, is collaborating with A. Sampaio, RDD Textiles, Tintex Textiles, FOV Fabrics, Utenos Trikotažas and Swisstex Direct to demonstrate how polyester recovered from post-consumer textile waste can be incorporated into commercially viable fabrics. The partnerships represent an important step in connecting Reju’s planned recycling operations with downstream textile manufacturing, helping to establish a supply chain for regenerated polyester. Reju is developing a chemical recycling process based on technology originating from IBM Research, designed to recover polyester from discarded textiles and return it to the textile supply chain without the quality limitations associated with conventional mechanical recycling. The company is progressing plans for a network of Regeneration Hubs capable of processing post-consumer polyester waste at industrial scale. Alongside establishing recycling capacity, Reju is seeking to demonstrate that its regenerated materials can be processed efficiently by existing textile manufacturers while meeting the quality and performance requirements of apparel brands. The six participating mills bring complementary manufacturing capabilities covering knitted and woven fabrics, dyeing, finishing and garment production. In Portugal, A. Sampaio contributes more than 75 years of experience in circular knitted fabrics, while RDD Textiles specialises in advanced knitted constructions, recycled and bio-based materials and innovative dyeing technologies. title: Nuyarn wins Performance Days Wool Award
title_ko: Nuyarn, Performance Days Wool Award 수상
summary: Nuyarn Technologies has received the 2026 Performance Days Wool Award for an innovative open-net fabric construction developed in collaboration with Takisada Corporation, highlighting the potential of advanced wool technologies for high-performance apparel. The award recognises a lightweight fabric structure designed to maximise breathability and manage moisture at the vapour stage, supporting improved comfort during demanding […] The post Nuyarn wins Performance Days Wool Award appeared first on Knitting Industry .
content: Nuyarn Technologies has received the 2026 Performance Days Wool Award for an innovative open-net fabric construction developed in collaboration with Takisada Corporation, highlighting the potential of advanced wool technologies for high-performance apparel. The award recognises a lightweight fabric structure designed to maximise breathability and manage moisture at the vapour stage, supporting improved comfort during demanding physical activity. The development combines Nuyarn’s proprietary yarn technology with specialist fabric engineering to extend the performance capabilities of natural fibres. “This award reflects our ongoing drive to push the boundaries of performance textiles. Alongside our partners at Takisada Corporation, it demonstrates what’s possible when continuous innovation, fabric development, and strong partnerships come together,” said Andy Wynne, CEO of Nuyarn. The open-net construction offers potential applications across a broad range of performance apparel, from ultralight summer endurance garments to technical base layers for high-intensity alpine activities. Its structure is designed to facilitate moisture vapour transfer while retaining the durability, elasticity and thermoregulation required in modern activewear. At the heart of the development is Nuyarn’s twist-free spinning technology, which differs from conventional wool processing methods that tightly twist fibres together. By reducing the constraints imposed by traditional spinning, the technology is designed to preserve more of wool’s natural performance characteristics. content: By MK Prabhakar For Sulochana Cotton Mills, sustainability has been more than a response to an industry-wide trend. Over the years, the Tirupur-based textile major has built a strong reputation for developing and adopting innovative solutions aimed at reducing waste and promoting circularity across the textile value chain. Its pioneering initiatives in PET bottle recycling and post-industrial waste recycling have been among the key highlights of this journey. Sabhari Girish, Head of Sustainability, Sulochana Cotton Mills With sustainability continuing to remain an important part of its growth strategy, Sulochana is now looking at taking its efforts a step further. The company is planning to expand its manufacturing footprint beyond its existing six units, while simultaneously investing in textile-to-textile recycling, smart manufacturing and garmenting. We caught up with Sabhari Girish, Head of Sustainability, Sulochana Cotton Mills, for an exclusive interaction to understand the company’s performance during FY 2025-26 and its plans for the coming years. summary: PORT ST. The concept gives a name to technical membranes—lightweight, flexible composite fabrics used across architecture for roofing, facades, […]
content: PORT ST. LUCIE, Fla. — November 5, 2026 — Serge Ferrari North America, the North American subsidiary of Serge Ferrari Group, which designs, develops, and manufactures innovative composite materials, introduces the 7th Material to the North American market. The concept gives a name to technical membranes—lightweight, flexible composite fabrics used across architecture for roofing, facades, shading, and interior applications. Beijing Taikang Yanyuan Health&Wellness Center Serge Ferrari Group unveiled the 7th Material at its global launch event on Sept. 24, 2026, establishing it as an open industry category rather than a product line or trademark. The concept positions technical membranes as a seventh construction material category, alongside stone, earth, wood, concrete, metal, and glass. “We are not launching a new product; we are giving a name to a material family that is already present in architecture but still insufficiently recognized,” said Sébastien Baril, CEO of Serge Ferrari Group. “With the 7th Material, we want to show that performance can also come from the behavior of a surface, its lightness, and its ability to combine multiple functions. This category is intended to be open, documented, and shared across the whole industry.” For nearly 50 years, technical membranes have been used in architecture, yet they are often grouped broadly with “lightweight” materials and specified only after a building has already been designed. The 7th Material concept aims to bring membranes into the design process earlier. While the six historic materials are classified by their composition, the 7th Material is defined by its function, deriving performance from a surface under tension rather than from mass and added layers. content: Detlef Fischer is the owner and CEO of TEXTILCOLOR AG, a Swiss specialty chemicals company based in Sevelen, Switzerland. Under his leadership, TEXTILCOLOR combines extensive expertise in textile chemistry with practical application technology and customer-specific solutions. The company supports its customers throughout the textile value chain — from pretreatment and dyeing to printing and the functional finishing and coating of textiles. TEXTILCOLOR stands for sustainable, environmentally friendly solutions, modern infrastructure and a clear focus on the future of sustainable textile production. Figure: Detlef Fischer is the owner and CEO of TEXTILCOLOR AG In an exclusive interview with Textile Today, Detlef Fischer shares his insights on textile chemical innovation, sustainable production practices and the evolving challenges and opportunities shaping the global textile industry. Textile Today: How is TEXTILCOLOR adapting its textile dyeing and finishing technologies to meet the industry’s growing demands for sustainability, resource efficiency and high performance? Detlef Fischer : We combine product innovation, application expertise and close cooperation with our customers to meet the new demands of our industry. Our objective is to develop solutions that deliver consistent technical performance while helping textile manufacturers reduce their environmental impact and use resources more efficiently. A key element is the development of highly effective dyes and textile auxiliaries that support more efficient dyeing and finishing processes. title: White House slashes production planning time
summary: Indian garment manufacturer White House has reduced its production planning cycle by 60–80% following the implementation of Coats Digital’s FastReactPlan software, improving production visibility, operational coordination and on-time delivery performance. The Chennai-based, vertically integrated manufacturer has introduced the solution to connect production planning, factory capacity, order scheduling, material requirements and pre-production activities within a single […] The post White House slashes production planning time appeared first on Knitting Industry .
content: Indian garment manufacturer White House has reduced its production planning cycle by 60–80% following the implementation of Coats Digital’s FastReactPlan software, improving production visibility, operational coordination and on-time delivery performance. The Chennai-based, vertically integrated manufacturer has introduced the solution to connect production planning, factory capacity, order scheduling, material requirements and pre-production activities within a single planning environment. The implementation has enabled faster decision-making and greater flexibility in responding to changing customer requirements. Established in 1962, White House employs approximately 4,000 people and operates 1,800 sewing machines across five manufacturing units. With a production capacity of around 800,000 garments per month and annual turnover of approximately US$65 million, the company supplies international brands including Ralph Lauren, GANT, Marco Polo and Timberland. Its manufacturing operations encompass knitting, fabric dyeing, garment dyeing, printing, embroidery and sewing, providing extensive control over the production process. Previously, White House relied heavily on spreadsheets, emails and information held across different departments and locations. By Nithin Kumar TITAS… The post TITAS at 30: Taiwan Turns Textile Innovation into Global Opportunity appeared first on The Textile Magazine .
content: The 2026 anniversary edition connected circular materials, performance fabrics and AI with international sourcing, showing how Taiwan’s textile expertise can serve the next generation of products. By Nithin Kumar TITAS 2026 made the connections between material development, garment design and factory performance easier to see. Its 30th edition paired recovered fibres and functional fabrics with finished concept garments and digital production tools, giving buyers concrete examples of how Taiwan’s textile capabilities can support their next product. Held from 6 to 8 October at Taipei Nangang Exhibition Center, Hall 1, the 30th Taipei Innovative Textile Application Show brought together 410 exhibitors from 12 countries across 977 booths. Organiser Taiwan Textile Federation (TTF) reported approximately 30,405 buyer visits over the three days and estimated future business opportunities at US$60 million. Since its debut in 1997, TITAS has given Taiwanese suppliers a shared platform for reaching international brands. Its 30th edition put that role into perspective: functional fabric development is increasingly connected with circular design and digital production, broadening the scope of the sourcing conversation. The sourcing programme connected more than 70 international brands from 16 markets with Taiwanese exhibitors in over 900 procurement meetings. Visiting delegations also came from India, Japan, South Korea, Vietnam and Thailand. The new Italian pavilion, organised by the Italian Trade Agency with ACIMIT, brought 11 machinery companies, including FADIS, Color Service, Corino and Danitech. title: YKK Explores Mould-Free Customisation With 3D-Printed Snap Caps
summary: The ISPO-recognised concept extends YKK’s work with Variloom from zipper pullers to snap caps, showing how digital fabrication could give brands more freedom over small but distinctive components. The post YKK Explores Mould-Free Customisation With 3D-Printed Snap Caps appeared first on The Interline .
content: YKK has won Best Product in the Accessories category at ISPO Textrends for a 3D-printed snap cap developed with Variloom. The concept combines YKK’s fastening expertise with an on-demand fabrication process that allows intricate textures and shapes to be produced without conventional moulds. YKK’s announcement While the snap cap is a concept rather than a commercial launch, it could prompt fashion product teams to think about the links between customisation and order size: YKK says the process can remove the moulding and minimum-order constraints that limit how freely brands can develop distinctive trims. The material adds another design dimension. The insert combines Variloom’s materials with Sulapac’s wood composite, cotton fibres and thermoplastic polyurethane. YKK says more than 55% of the insert is bio-based, using Sulapac’s material specifications, and describes a surface intended to look and feel more natural. YKK and Variloom previously developed a 3D Composite Puller, covered by The Interline in April , with customisable shape, texture, colour and branding. The snap cap extends that approach into another fastening component. Variloom’s wider system also provides useful context for how this might develop into a production workflow. Its design software controls the printer’s path, while a separate operating system manages jobs and progress across a fleet of printers. The company is developing the design and production infrastructure alongside the materials. For brands, the opportunity is to make variation easier to accommodate. A common printing process could support different designs across capsule collections, collaborations or regional ranges, reducing the need to commit each variation to its own mould. title: Could A Cultural And Political Pendulum-Swing Undermine Fashion’s Big Visions For AI?
summary: A holiday season shaped by hand-drawn initiatives, a decisive leftward swing in US elections, and a historic market slump all seem to suggest a new stage of anti-AI sentiment. At the same time, it’s becoming more deeply embedded in industry practice. The post Could A Cultural And Political Pendulum-Swing Undermine Fashion’s Big Visions For AI? appeared first on The Interline .
content: Key Takeaways A political swing in the USA which seems, at least in part, to also have been a referendum on data centre construction; a technology-market sell-off; and a pair of luxury campaigns celebrating human craft all expose the gap between the AI industry’s ambitions and the public support it needs to realise them. Consumers’ public resistance to AI coexists with a growing willingness to use it for search and shopping research, according to new McKinsey research. Trust in agents making purchases may remain lower, but evidence continues to suggest that consumers have a quixotic relationship with the technology that complicates an easy read of the zeitgeist. Practically speaking, the legislative mandate is likely to have a greater long-term impact than consumer attitudes. And that mandate is being served at precisely the same time that AI is becoming more embedded in fashion business models, as evidenced by Stitch Fix’s showcase of how proprietary customer data can inform private-label product creation and assortment decisions. The Interline doesn’t deal in politics, but as a technology publication it’s hard to avoid the association between electoral issues and AI build-out, which seem to have become synonymous with one another over the last few months – coming to a head in this week’s US midterms, which, in a very real sense, put some strong arguments against AI infrastructure onto local ballots . Despite a lot of coverage claiming the contrary , there’s little hard evidence to suggest that the pronounced swing in American politics was a direct repudiation of AI, or “big tech”. summary: Bangladesh’s textile and apparel industry is entering a period where cost competitiveness alone will no longer be enough to secure future growth. Rising production costs, changing buyer expectations...
content: Bangladesh’s textile and apparel industry is entering a period where cost competitiveness alone will no longer be enough to secure future growth. Rising production costs, changing buyer expectations, rapid technological advancement and the growing demand for higher-value and sustainable products are pushing the industry to build stronger capabilities in knowledge, research and innovation. Figure: Prof. Dr. Engr. Ayub Nabi Khan,Vice Chancellor, BGMEA University of Fashion & Technology (BUFT) & Member of the Steering Board, Textile Innovation Exchange (TIE). For Prof. Dr. Engr. Ayub Nabi Khan , Vice Chancellor of BGMEA University of Fashion & Technology (BUFT), this transition will depend heavily on how effectively Bangladesh connects industry with academia. He believes universities must move closer to factory realities, strengthen research in advanced materials and technologies, and prepare engineers for AI, automation, digital manufacturing, sustainability and product diversification. Speaking to Textile Today , Prof. Khan discusses the skills Bangladesh needs to compete on value, the gap between textile education and modern manufacturing, the commercialization of academic research, opportunities in MMF and technical textiles, and the need for deeper industry-academia collaboration. He also highlights the role of platforms such as Textile Innovation Exchange (TIE) and the upcoming TIE–ITET Textile Innovation Expo 2026 in bringing researchers, factories, engineers, technology providers and young innovators closer together. title: Dry Powder Impregnation vs. Traditional Saturation: Rethinking How Functional Materials Are Applied
summary: By Will Motchar, President & CEO, Navis TubeTex For decades, wet saturation has been one of the textile industry’s standard methods for applying functional chemistry: Immerse the material. Control the… The post Dry Powder Impregnation vs. Traditional Saturation: Rethinking How Functional Materials Are Applied appeared first on The Textile Magazine .
content: By Will Motchar, President & CEO, Navis TubeTex For decades, wet saturation has been one of the textile industry’s standard methods for applying functional chemistry: Immerse the material. Control the wet pickup. Remove the excess. Then evaporate the water through drying and curing. It’s proven technology—and for many applications, it remains the right solution. Will Motchar, President & CEO, Navis TubeTex But today’s manufacturers are facing a different set of challenges: rising energy and raw-material costs, pressure to reduce water consumption, increasingly demanding performance requirements, and a growing focus on sustainability. That raises an important question: If water isn’t part of the finished product, do we always need to introduce it into the process? A Different Approach Fibroline dry powder impregnation technology takes a fundamentally different approach. Instead of using water as the carrier for functional chemistry, controlled electric fields are used to introduce dry functional particles directly into porous materials. The particles can penetrate into the structure of the substrate and are subsequently fixed in place. This creates the potential to incorporate materials such as: Activated carbon and adsorbents Superabsorbent powders Flame-retardant materials Antimicrobial additives Phase-change materials Conductive particles Catalytic materials Specialty binders and functional powders The objective isn’t simply to eliminate water. It’s to put the functional material where it is needed, in the quantity needed, with greater control over the process.
