content: Fashion’s next looming AI challenge has nothing to do with uptake. In the survey portion of The Interline’s AI Report 2026 , we found that only around a quarter of respondents trusted AI’s output enough to base critical decisions on top of, and we identified a prevailing concern amongst practitioners that companies (and especially innovation leaders) are overestimating the capabilities of artificial intelligence and the extent of automation. It’s clear from the data that fashion’s spending on AI is set to keep rising, but access to the technology is evidently not the same thing as establishing trust – either in its standalone capabilities, or in its place at the heart of brands’, retailers’ and makers’ technology estates. On 15th October 2026, The Interline brought together three executives to examine that gap across product and line creation, strategic sourcing and production, and consumer-facing content. title: Wage issue in RMG sector: An alternative proposition
summary: Minimum wage enhancement in Bangladesh’s Ready-Made Garment (RMG) sector is economically and socially justified. Rising prices of essential commodities, housing, healthcare, and transportation, couple...
content: Minimum wage enhancement in Bangladesh’s Ready-Made Garment (RMG) sector is economically and socially justified. Rising prices of essential commodities, housing, healthcare, and transportation, coupled with inflation and BDT depreciation, continue to erode workers’ purchasing power. Therefore, nominal wage increases alone cannot ensure improved living standards. A sustainable solution requires coordinated reforms balancing workers’ welfare, industrial competitiveness, and productivity rather than relying solely on periodic wage revisions. Alternative and sustainable solutions Decentralization of factories: Encourage new RMG investments outside Dhaka through improved infrastructure, energy, transport, housing, and targeted incentives. This would reduce living costs, ease pressure on Dhaka, and promote regional development. Regional minimum wages: Introduce a transparent wage structure reflecting regional living costs, particularly housing, food, and transportation, while protecting workers’ basic living standards and ensuring equal pay for comparable work. Minimum wage benchmark in USD: Consider announcing an internationally comparable USD wage benchmark alongside legally guaranteed BDT payments. A transparent conversion mechanism and periodic review should address exchange-rate fluctuations and improve international wage comparisons. Inflation control: Strengthen market monitoring, control artificial price increases, improve supply chains, and stabilize essential commodity prices. Periodic cost-of-living adjustments should protect workers’ real purchasing power. Productivity and fair buyer pricing: Invest in workers’ skills, mid-level management, technology, and production efficiency. content: Italian yarn manufacturer Fulgar has highlighted the potential of bio-based synthetic fibres to reduce the textile industry’s dependence on fossil resources, while emphasising the need for greater transparency, reliable certification and competitive pricing to support their wider adoption. The company contributed to an international discussion on the future of biosynthetics at the recent Performance Days exhibition in Munich, Germany, where Daniela Antunes, Fulgar’s Marketing Manager, joined industry experts to examine the opportunities and challenges associated with renewable raw materials. The panel discussion, entitled From Fossil to Vegetal: The Promises and Challenges of Biosynthetics , brought together representatives from Fulgar, Indorama Ventures, ISCC PLUS and Noosa. Moderated by Sophie Bramel, Technical Editor at Sportstextiles, the session explored the technical, environmental and commercial considerations influencing the development and adoption of biopolymers in textile applications. Central to Fulgar’s contribution was its ongoing research into next-generation polyamide yarns, particularly EVO and Q-GEO, two developments designed to combine renewable raw materials with the performance characteristics required by contemporary textile markets. EVO is a 100% bio-based yarn developed and manufactured by Fulgar using renewable feedstocks derived equally from castor oil and industrial corn. The castor oil originates from crops cultivated in arid regions that do not compete with food production, while the corn component comes from industrial crops not intended for human consumption. content: Swiss automotive supplier Autoneum is to acquire the French Trèves Group in a deal that will significantly expand its global manufacturing operations and strengthen its position in automotive acoustic and thermal insulation, interior trim and luggage compartment solutions. The acquisition will bring together two established suppliers to the international automotive industry, creating a business with combined annual revenues expected to exceed CHF 2.9 billion (€3.1 billion) in 2026. Trèves, which generated revenues of approximately €720 million in 2025, employs around 4,600 people across 26 production facilities in 15 countries in Europe, North and South America, Asia and Africa. The company has longstanding relationships with major automotive manufacturers and specialises in acoustic and thermal management systems and interior components. Under the agreement announced on November 2nd, Autoneum will pay approximately €40 million upfront, with a further performance-related payment of up to €24 million possible depending on improvements in profitability and the achievement of synergies by 2029. More than 80% of the initial consideration will be settled through newly issued Autoneum shares, with approximately €7.5 million paid in cash. The shares will be subject to a three-year lock-up period. The transaction is expected to be completed in early 2027, subject to consultation with the relevant employee representative bodies and customary regulatory approvals. The planned takeover follows Autoneum’s €117 million acquisition of the automotive business of Germany’s Borgers Group in April 2023. title: Luxury Brands Know Their Buyers. Do They Know Their Customers?
summary: Product authentication has been luxury's primary use case for blockchain, but so far it's focused on visibility at the point of sale or resale. A tech founder argues it has a deeper role to play. The post Luxury Brands Know Their Buyers. Do They Know Their Customers? appeared first on The Interline .
content: Luxury brands have become remarkably good at understanding the people who buy their products. Sophisticated CRM systems, loyalty programs, and digital analytics give them a precise picture of purchasing behaviours, spending patterns, and customer preferences. Brands and maisons know, in exacting detail, who their best clients are, what they buy, how often they shop, and what they are likely to want next. They use this to put some of the world’s most sophisticated clienteling operations into practice, for the planet’s most discerning shoppers. What they have comparatively little visibility into is what happens to the products they buy after the point of sale, and the extended lives those products (which are uniquely designed for longevity, timeless style, and are seen as a store of value) now live. Products perceived as perennially stylish and valuable now no longer just get passed from one generation to the next: they circulate through resale platforms, auction houses, consignment boutiques, and private collectors, creating a second life that most brands cannot see until the item comes back into their ecosystem for service, repair, or authentication. That secondary market is no longer a fringe economy alongside luxury retail; st’s part of the system, and also part of the buying decision matrix for a growing cohort of luxury shoppers who purchase goods with the intention of parting with them afterwards. For an expanding group of consumers, the secondary market is also where their relationship with luxury begins. A first-time buyer may enter the category through a pre-owned handbag, rather than the traditional route of a gateway product like a scarf, a belt, or a fragrance. content: German circular knitting machinery manufacturer Terrot Textilmaschinen will highlight its UCC 672-ME double-electronic jacquard machine at ITMA Asia + CITME 2026 in Shanghai, China, from 20-24 November, demonstrating its capabilities for premium mattress ticking, upholstery and technical textiles. The Chemnitz-based company, part of the Santoni China Group, will present a 38-inch diameter, E20 gauge machine equipped with 88 feeders at stand H4.1 C39. The exhibition configuration will feature a specialised mattress fabric incorporating cooling yarns, differentiated comfort zones and knitted structures designed to promote ventilation on both surfaces. UCC 672-ME The UCC 672-ME features independently programmable three-way needle selection on both cylinder and dial, allowing manufacturers to control knit, tuck and miss actions at every feeder. This enables intricate jacquard patterns, three-dimensional textures, ventilation zones and reversible structures without the limitations of conventional mechanical patterning systems. content: The Institution of Textile Engineers and Technologists (ITET) Bangladesh has called for urgent government action to restore stability and strengthen industrial security amid rising labour unrest in the textile and RMG sector. The organization stressed the need for uninterrupted production to safeguard Bangladesh’s key export industry and maintain investor confidence. In a statement, ITET Bangladesh expressed deep concern over recent incidents of arson, vandalism, labour unrest, protests and road blockades in different industrial areas, saying these incidents have severely disrupted normal factory operations and production. The organization noted that many factories have already shut down, raising concerns over the country's economy, employment and export trade. According to ITET Bangladesh, the industry was attempting to recover from prolonged gas crises and other challenges when the fresh wave of instability created further uncertainty about its future. It also warned that continued unrest could undermine the confidence of international buyers and investors and damage Bangladesh's image in the global market. Emphasizing the importance of protecting workers' legitimate rights and demands, ITET Bangladesh said factory security, a stable production environment and the rule of law must also be ensured. The organization called for resolving the underlying causes of labour unrest through dialogue between workers and factory owners. It also urged the authorities to conduct impartial investigations to identify those involved in arson, vandalism, looting and sabotage and bring them to justice. title: Government announces new wage board for garment workers
summary: On November 1, the Bangladesh government has formed a new wage board to determine revised minimum wages for readymade garment (RMG) workers amid ongoing labor unrest and demands for a monthly minimum...
content: On November 1, the Bangladesh government has formed a new wage board to determine revised minimum wages for readymade garment (RMG) workers amid ongoing labor unrest and demands for a monthly minimum wage of Tk 30,000. The six-member board, constituted under the Ministry of Labour and Employment, is chaired by Sheikh Ashfaqur Rahman, a senior district and sessions judge. The board includes five members representing employers, workers and the independent category. Prof. Mosleh Uddin Ahmed of the Department of Public Administration at the University of Dhaka has been appointed as the independent member. Employer representatives include Asif Ayub, Joint Secretary-General of the Bangladesh Employers’ Federation, and A.B.M. Shamsuddin, Director of the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA). Worker representatives are Anwar Hossain, President of Bangladesh Jatiyatabadi Sramik Dal, and Babul Akhter, General Secretary of the Bangladesh Garments and Industrial Workers Federation. The appointments were announced through separate notifications issued under the Bangladesh Labour Act, 2006, as amended in 2026. The chairman has been instructed to initiate the process of fixing the minimum wage in consultation with all stakeholders. Labour and Employment Minister Ariful Haque Choudhury announced the formation of the board, stating that it has been tasked with recommending a revised wage structure within six months. The review comes three years after the last wage revision in 2023, when the minimum monthly wage for garment workers was set at Tk 12,500. content: Key Insights Fuel prices are forecast to rise 32% in 2026. Brent crude may average $91/barrel, up from $69 in 2025. Further conflict could push Brent to $105/barrel in 2027. Global food prices may rise 18% over 2026–27. Supply disruptions could worsen global inflation and food insecurity. Global fuel prices are projected to rise by 32% in 2026, driven by escalating conflicts in the Middle East, the Russia-Ukraine war and supply disruptions, according to the World Bank’s October 2026 Commodity Markets Outlook. The report forecasts that overall commodity prices will increase by an average of 23% this year, with energy costs accounting for a significant share of the rise. Brent crude oil is expected to average $91 per barrel in 2026, up from $69 in 2025. However, prices are projected to ease to $79 per barrel in 2027 if geopolitical tensions subside and supply conditions improve. The World Bank said the conflict in the Middle East has delivered a major shock to global energy supplies. Declining oil inventories have increased the risk that further disruptions could intensify supply shortages and push prices higher. The Russia-Ukraine war has added to market pressure by disrupting energy and food supplies. Restrictions on Russia’s refined petroleum production and exports, alongside interruptions to grain shipments through the Black Sea, have further increased uncertainty in global commodity markets. Despite the expected decline in overall commodity prices in 2027, the outlook remains vulnerable to further escalation in the Middle East. Meanwhile, the World Bank warned that, under a more adverse scenario, Brent crude could average $105 per barrel in 2027, significantly above its baseline forecast of $79. content: On 30 October, Global crude oil prices surged more than 2%, reaching their highest levels in six months as concerns over a possible escalation of the Iran conflict heightened fears of supply disruptions. Investors are increasingly worried that the conflict could worsen following the US midterm elections, raising uncertainty over global oil supplies. Brent crude futures for December delivery settled at $117.64 per barrel on 30 October, up 2.4% from the previous session. During the trading session, prices briefly climbed above $118 per barrel. Meanwhile, US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude rose 2.1% to settle at $104.12 per barrel. Oil prices also recorded strong gains throughout October. Brent crude increased by 13.6% during the month, while WTI rose 15.2%, reflecting growing concerns over geopolitical risks and potential supply disruptions. Tensions surrounding oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz have further intensified market concerns. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) reported four incidents involving supertankers within a single day. According to the IRGC, two tankers were damaged by mines while travelling through routes prohibited by Iranian authorities. The Strait of Hormuz is one of the world's most important energy shipping routes, handling a significant volume of global crude oil and fuel transportation. Any conflict or security threat in the waterway could disrupt shipments and put further pressure on international oil supplies. summary: Key Insights Bangladesh RMG sector faces a $4.8 billion funding gap to meet 2030 climate goals. Australian clean energy delegations explore battery storage partnerships to stabilize factory power. De...
content: Key Insights Bangladesh RMG sector faces a $4.8 billion funding gap to meet 2030 climate goals. Australian clean energy delegations explore battery storage partnerships to stabilize factory power. Denmark and Sweden support a 500 MW offshore wind project off Cox's Bazar. Natural gas shortages and LNG spot prices near $30 per MMBtu raise operational costs. Rooftop solar cannot power wet processing, requiring heat recovery and electrification. Bangladesh's ready-made garment industry is partnering with global fashion brands, renewable energy companies, and international development partners to adopt solar power, offshore wind, battery storage, and energy-efficient machinery. Manufacturers are making this shift to handle high energy costs, gas shortages, and strict carbon reduction demands from international buyers. However, realizing this green transition requires substantial capital expenditure. According to LightCastle Partners, Bangladesh's RMG sector requires $6.6 billion between 2025 and 2029 to achieve a 50 percent reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030. With only $1.6 billion in funding secured to date, the sector faces a massive $4.8 billion financing gap that demands urgent expansion of international climate finance, soft loans, and concessionary funding mechanisms. To bridge the financial shortfall and accelerate on-site clean energy, international solar investments and technology transfers are expanding rapidly across Bangladesh's apparel sector. Denmark's Heartland and fashion giant BESTSELLER are funding solar decarbonization models through a partnership with local cleantech venture SOLshare. title: Garment workers resume protests in Gazipur demanding Tk30,000 minimum wage
summary: Garment workers staged fresh protests in several areas of Gazipur on Sunday, demanding an increase in the minimum monthly wage to Tk30,000. The demonstrations and road blockades brought traffic on the...
content: Garment workers staged fresh protests in several areas of Gazipur on Sunday, demanding an increase in the minimum monthly wage to Tk30,000. The demonstrations and road blockades brought traffic on the Dhaka–Tangail Highway to a standstill, while protesters set fire to a police box in Konabari. Five platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) personnel have been deployed to maintain law and order amid the unrest. On the morning of 01 November, workers took to the streets in Safipur Bazar, Chandra Palli Bidyut, Mouchak and Telichala areas of Kaliakair upazila, staging demonstrations and chanting slogans demanding higher wages. According to Kaliakair Police Station Officer-in-Charge (OC) Shahidul Islam, workers had occupied the highway since morning, disrupting traffic on the busy route. Gazipur Deputy Commissioner Md. Nurul Karim Bhuiyan said five platoons of BGB personnel had been deployed in view of the situation. The number could be increased if necessary. In Konabari, agitated workers set fire to a police box located in the middle of the highway. They reportedly removed items from the police box and set those on fire as well, said Konabari Police Station OC Iftekhar Hossain. The protests come after nearly two weeks of demonstrations by garment workers in different parts of Gazipur over wage increases. On 31 October, workers blocked the highway around Chandra Palli Bidyut and Gate No. 3 of the Ansar Academy in Kaliakair until around 8:30 pm. Police later dispersed them using tear gas and batons. Traffic returned to normal after nearly five hours. On Sunday morning, workers from Karni Knit Composite, Knit Asia and several nearby factories in the Ratanpur area of Kaliakair reported to their workplaces but did not join production. summary: Danish garment maker Spectre has inaugurated a new green factory in Hung Yen Province, northern Vietnam, expanding its manufacturing footprint in the country while helping reduce greenhouse gas emissions through energy-efficient production, according to the Danish Embassy in Vietnam. The new facility, Spectre Hung Yen 2, opened at Song Tra Industrial Park in Thai Binh […] The post Danish garment firm Spectre opens $30mn green factory in northern Vietnam appeared first on Textile Focus .
content: Danish garment maker Spectre has inaugurated a new green factory in Hung Yen Province, northern Vietnam, expanding its manufacturing footprint in the country while helping reduce greenhouse gas emissions through energy-efficient production, according to the Danish Embassy in Vietnam. The new facility, Spectre Hung Yen 2, opened at Song Tra Industrial Park in Thai Binh Ward on Friday, marking the company’s fourth factory in Vietnam and second in Hung Yen. With nearly 80 years of experience in the garment industry, Spectre specializes in producing functional apparel for premium sportswear and outdoor brands. Backed by an investment of US$30 million, the new factory is expected to cut carbon dioxide emissions by approximately 1,600 metric tons annually compared with conventional factories of a similar size. It has received LEED Gold certification, the third-highest certification level under the Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design (LEED) rating system developed by the U.S. Green Building Council. The facility combines solar power with modern design solutions to improve energy efficiency and reduce its environmental footprint. It is also equipped with advanced machinery and technologies, including automation and artificial intelligence (AI) solutions, to improve production efficiency and establish higher standards across Spectre’s manufacturing operations. The factory is expected to create jobs for around 3,000 local workers. Jesper Klausen, Spectre’s co-owner and chief business development officer, said the company, was proud of its latest investment in Hung Yen. title: 12 European countries to release 42.6mn barrels of oil from strategic reserves
summary: Twelve European countries have announced plans to release 42.6 million barrels of oil from their strategic reserves by the end of January 2027 to ease concerns over global energy supplies. The release...
content: Twelve European countries have announced plans to release 42.6 million barrels of oil from their strategic reserves by the end of January 2027 to ease concerns over global energy supplies. The release will include approximately 20.5 million barrels of diesel, accounting for nearly half of the total volume. The announcement was made in a joint statement on 29 October. EU Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen told reporters that member states had reaffirmed their commitment to rapidly releasing the oil reserves over the coming months, with a significant portion allocated to diesel. Courtesy: Collected The participating countries are France, Germany, Italy, Belgium, Denmark, Greece, Latvia, Lithuania, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal and Sweden. The initiative is part of an agreement reached among G7 countries earlier this month. A few weeks before the latest announcement, G7 economies had announced plans to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil to stabilize global supplies. The International Energy Agency (IEA) had also urged its member countries in mid-October to increase oil supplies from strategic reserves ahead of the winter season. All 12 countries participating in the latest initiative are IEA members. The move comes amid a sharp rise in global energy prices following the war involving the United States, Israel and Iran. The conflict has increased pressure on energy costs across Europe and the United States, raising concerns among consumers and policymakers. High energy prices have also become a significant political issue for the Trump administration ahead of next week's US congressional elections.
